blocks.text: A **computer generation** is a broad stage of technological development, mainly identified by major changes in **processing hardware**. The boundaries overlap, because newer technology did not instantly replace older machines.

blocks.title: Technology path of the generations
items: Vacuum tubes
1st generation
Transistors
2nd generation
Integrated circuits
3rd generation
Microprocessors / VLSI
4th generation
AI-oriented computing
5th generation

blocks.title: Key technologies
rows: Electronic device that controls electron flow inside an evacuated enclosure; early electronic computers used tubes for switching and amplification
Semiconductor device that switches or amplifies electronic signals; smaller size, lower power use and better reliability let it replace tubes
Interconnected components, including transistors and resistors, fabricated on a small semiconductor chip; silicon is the most common base material
Very Large-Scale Integration: very large numbers of transistors on one chip
Ultra Large-Scale Integration: a historical label for still higher density; exact numerical thresholds vary, and modern chips hold billions of transistors
An integrated circuit that implements CPU processing functions; its switching elements are transistors, but the whole processor is not a single switch

blocks.title: Semiconductor or transistor?
blocks.text: When both 'semiconductors' and 'transistors' appear as options for what replaced vacuum tubes, choose the more specific answer: **transistors**.

blocks.title: The five generations (textbook ranges)
rows: ENIAC, EDVAC, EDSAC, UNIVAC I, IBM 650, IBM 701
IBM 1620, IBM 7094, CDC 1604, CDC 3600, IBM 1400 series
IBM System/360, System/370, ICL 2900, selected DEC PDP models

blocks.title: Dates to remember
items: First generation: vacuum tubes
Second generation: transistors
Third generation: integrated circuits
Nov 1971
Intel 4004, first commercially available single-chip microprocessor
Fourth generation (this convention): microprocessors and VLSI
1980 onwards
Fifth generation: AI and knowledge-processing emphasis
Japan's formal fifth-generation project begins

blocks.title: Accuracy note
blocks.text: These are **textbook ranges, not universal cutoffs**. Commercial microprocessors arrived in 1971 and microprocessor computing continues today, so many books start the fourth generation at 1971. Fifth-generation aims overlap with this technology.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: First = tubes, Second = transistors, Third = ICs, Fourth = microprocessors, Fifth = AI emphasis. Think T-T-I-M-A.

blocks.title: Features (textbook period 1940-1956)
items: Large machines that used **vacuum tubes** for electronic switching.
Needed substantial electricity and cooling and required frequent maintenance.
Programs relied heavily on machine-level instructions.
Punched cards and paper tape were common input media; printed or punched results were the output.
Main memory differed by machine: magnetic drums, mercury delay lines and electrostatic storage were used. Magnetic-core memory was not universal.

blocks.title: Examples and facts
rows: ENIAC, EDVAC, EDSAC, UNIVAC I, IBM 650, IBM 701
Used a magnetic drum as main memory
Basic exam charts often describe first-generation operation in milliseconds

blocks.title: Harvard Mark I
blocks.text: **Harvard Mark I** was electromechanical. It was an early computing milestone, but not a vacuum-tube electronic computer.

blocks.title: Features (textbook period 1957-1963)
items: **Transistors** replaced vacuum tubes as the principal switching components.
Computers generally became smaller, more reliable and less power-hungry.
Magnetic-core main memory became widespread; magnetic tapes and disks supported storage.
Assembly language was important, and FORTRAN and COBOL also became established.
Punched-card input and printed output remained common.
Elementary comparison charts often associate operation times with microseconds.

blocks.title: Examples and terms
rows: IBM 1620, IBM 7094, CDC 1604, CDC 3600 and IBM 1400-series machines
Uses symbolic instructions and is translated by an assembler
Jobs are collected and run with little user interaction during execution

blocks.text: Batch systems were particularly important in the second-generation era, but **batch processing is not exclusive to one generation**.

blocks.title: Features (textbook period 1964-1971)
items: **Integrated-circuit** technology increased component density and improved speed, reliability and processing capacity.
Multiprogramming and time-sharing became increasingly important.
Keyboards and display terminals supported interactive use.
Core memory remained significant; semiconductor memory developed during the transition to later systems.
Magnetic disks and tape were widely used.

blocks.title: Examples
rows: IBM System/360, IBM System/370, ICL 2900 and selected DEC PDP models

blocks.title: Caution on examples
blocks.text: Many System/360 models used hybrid **Solid Logic Technology** modules. PDP was a family spanning different technological periods, so its generation depends on the model.

blocks.title: Features
items: **Microprocessors** brought CPU functions onto a single integrated circuit.
Increasing **VLSI** density supported compact, affordable personal computers.
Semiconductor RAM and ROM became standard.
Storage expanded through hard disks, floppy disks, optical media and flash devices.
Keyboards, mice, scanners, displays and printers supported interaction.
Networking and graphical interfaces became widespread.

blocks.title: Examples and facts
rows: Apple II and IBM-compatible PCs; Apple I is also cited as a fourth-era example
Introduced in November 1971; widely recognised as the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor

blocks.title: Unreliable chart labels
blocks.text: A chart entry named 'STAR 1000' has an unclear intended model, so do not memorise it as a verified generation marker. Labels such as 'i3-i11' are also not a reliable generation classification.

blocks.title: Fifth-generation emphasis
items: Artificial intelligence (AI)
Expert systems and knowledge-based systems
Neural networks
Natural language processing
Parallel processing
Intelligent robotics

blocks.title: Terms
rows: Combined knowledge information processing, large-scale parallel processing and logic programming
Knowledge Information Processing System; it describes a processing approach, not an input/output device

blocks.text: **VLSI/ULSI** describe how densely chips are integrated, while **AI** describes computational methods and applications. These ideas overlap.

blocks.title: Important distinction
blocks.text: **Pentium 4** and **AMD Athlon** are processor families. **Desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone** are device categories. None of them alone defines a fifth-generation computer.

sections.title: Memory and Storage Through the Generations

blocks.title: Memory development
rows: Drums, delay lines and electrostatic storage; core memory appeared later
Core remained important while semiconductor memory emerged
Semiconductor RAM and ROM became standard

blocks.text: No generation used only one memory or storage technology.

blocks.title: Secondary storage
rows: Magnetic tape and magnetic disks were important throughout
Holographic Versatile Disc, a specialised holographic optical-storage format
USB drives, memory cards and most modern SSDs

blocks.text: Microprocessor-era systems added widespread optical and flash storage. Modern computers use SSDs, hard disks and network or cloud storage. **SSDs are not exclusive to the fifth generation.**

blocks.title: Categories
rows: A portable microprocessor-based personal computer, usually operated by touch
A historical class smaller and less expensive than mainframes; many supported multiple users
Supports demanding organisational workloads, large-scale data processing and many concurrent activities

blocks.text: **Desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone** identify form or use, not a unique hardware generation.

blocks.title: Languages and their purpose
rows: Binary instructions executed by a processor
Symbolic instructions translated by an assembler
Web scripting and broader application uses
Database definition, queries and data manipulation
Numerical computation and technical programming; named from Matrix Laboratory
Symbolic processing and AI; named from List Processing
Logic programming and AI; named from Programming in Logic

blocks.title: Chronology check
blocks.text: FORTRAN became established in **1957**, Lisp originated in the late 1950s and C appeared in **1972**. A language cannot be assigned exclusively to one hardware generation.

blocks.title: Time units (smaller means shorter)
rows: Millions of Instructions Per Second; used when discussing processor or mainframe capacity

blocks.title: Exam-chart caution
blocks.text: Charts link first to milliseconds, second to microseconds, third to nanoseconds, fourth to picoseconds and fifth to femtoseconds. This is an oversimplified comparison, not a universal rule, and **MIPS** is not a complete measure of real application performance.

sections.title: Operating Systems, Interfaces, I/O and Networks

blocks.title: Operating-system development
items: Single-task
One main task at a time
Batch systems
Jobs run with little interaction
Multiprogramming
Several programs stay in memory
Time-sharing
Processing time split among users
Distributed and cloud
Connected computers, shared services

blocks.title: OS approaches
rows: Several programs stay in memory; the CPU changes work when necessary
Processing time is divided among tasks or users for interactive service
Computing resources and services are supplied through networks

blocks.text: These approaches coexist rather than replacing one another completely.

blocks.title: User interfaces
rows: Command-Line Interface: users enter text commands
Graphical User Interface: windows, icons, menus and other visual controls
Commonly Character User Interface: a text-based interface that can still run on modern machines

blocks.text: The broad trend is command-line, then graphical, then touch, then voice and AI-assisted interaction. All of them remain in use.

blocks.title: Input and output
rows: Punched cards, paper tape, printers and punched output
Keyboard, mouse, scanner, monitor and printer
Touchscreens, cameras, microphones, sensors and voice

blocks.text: A **touchscreen provides both input and output**. LCD/LED displays and colour printers are not generation-exclusive.

blocks.title: Network development
items: Standalone systems
Single machines
LAN
Local Area Network, a limited area
WAN
Wide Area Network, larger areas
Internet
Global network of networks
Cloud computing
Network access to computing resources

blocks.title: Processing methods
rows: Multiple processing units handle different parts of the work simultaneously
Work is coordinated across separate networked computers

blocks.text: LANs and WANs remain part of modern networks. Modern systems combine sequential and parallel execution, and speed gains depend on the workload. The **WWW** and **e-commerce** are services or applications, not defining hardware components of a generation.

blocks.title: Artificial intelligence
rows: Combines sensing, control and sometimes AI
Natural Language Processing: methods for analysing, interpreting and generating human language

blocks.title: NLP examples
items: Chatbots answer questions.
Google Translate converts text between languages.
Voice assistants interpret spoken requests such as 'Play music'.
Spam filters can analyse language to identify unwanted email.
Predictive typing suggests words; autocorrect fixes likely spelling errors.
Speech applications combine language processing with speech-recognition technology.

blocks.title: Quantum computing
rows: Uses quantum-mechanical principles to process information
Can be prepared in a superposition of the states associated with 0 and 1
In the computational basis it gives one result, 0 or 1
Use superposition, interference and sometimes entanglement

blocks.title: Common quantum myths
blocks.text: Quantum computers may beat classical methods for particular problems, not every task. Superposition does not let a computer display every answer at once, and quantum search is not simply trying all passwords at the same time. Traffic routing and optimisation are research applications with no guaranteed speed advantage.

blocks.title: The informal 'sixth generation'
rows: Some textbooks bundle quantum computing, nanotechnology, Internet of Things, advanced parallel processing and higher chip density under this label
There is no universally accepted sixth-generation definition or starting date
Internet of Things: connected physical devices with sensors, software and communication capabilities

blocks.text: 'UULSI = Ultra-squared Large-Scale Integration' is not a standard generation-defining term. If a question calls quantum technology 'sixth generation', treat that as a teaching convention.

blocks.title: Milestones
items: Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulation used for the US Census
21 June 1948
Manchester Baby (SSEM) runs the first program stored in electronic memory
EDSAC begins operating at Cambridge, giving an early practical stored-program computing service
Jack Kilby demonstrates a working semiconductor circuit
Robert Noyce develops the practical monolithic silicon IC concept
Nov 1971
Intel 4004 introduced
Apple I, designed by Steve Wozniak, is demonstrated

blocks.title: Details behind the dates
items: **Stored-program concept:** program instructions are kept in memory for automatic fetching and execution.
For an unrestricted question on the first electronic stored-program computer, distinguish **Manchester Baby**; EDSAC is the early practical service.
**Kilby and Noyce** are both recognised as IC co-inventors. Most conventional ICs use silicon.
**Punched cards:** holes in stiff cards encode information for machine reading. Punched-card control existed earlier in textile machinery such as Jacquard looms.
Hollerith's contribution was data-processing tabulation, not inventing every punched card.
**Apple I:** Wozniak and Steve Jobs helped bring it to market.

blocks.text: Remember the pairs: Kilby = 1958, Noyce = 1959, Baby = 1948, EDSAC = 1949, Hollerith = 1890, Apple I = 1976.

revision: A generation is a broad stage of hardware development; boundaries overlap and the dates are textbook ranges.
First: 1940-1956, vacuum tubes. Second: 1957-1963, transistors. Third: 1964-1971, integrated circuits.
Fourth: microprocessors and VLSI (1972-1979 in this convention); fifth: 1980 onwards, AI and knowledge processing.
ENIAC used about 18,000 vacuum tubes; Harvard Mark I was electromechanical, not a tube computer.
If both semiconductors and transistors are options for replacing tubes, choose transistors.
Second generation: assembly language, FORTRAN, COBOL, magnetic-core memory and batch processing.
Third generation: ICs, multiprogramming and time-sharing; IBM System/360, System/370 and ICL 2900 are listed examples.
Intel 4004 (November 1971) is recognised as the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor.
VLSI = Very Large-Scale Integration; ULSI = Ultra Large-Scale Integration; KIPS = Knowledge Information Processing System.
Japan's formal fifth-generation project began in 1982.
Pentium 4 and AMD Athlon are processor families; desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone are device categories.
Time units shrink: millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond, picosecond (10^-12 s), femtosecond (10^-15 s).
Manchester Baby (SSEM) ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948; EDSAC started in 1949.
Kilby demonstrated a working semiconductor circuit in 1958; Noyce developed the monolithic silicon IC in 1959.
Hollerith's punched-card tabulation was used in the 1890 US Census; Jacquard looms used punched-card control earlier.
A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1; measurement gives one result; 'sixth generation' has no universal definition.
